How many clips should I validate?

Source: vignettes/validation-effort.Rmd
validation-effort.Rmd

Manual review is the most expensive step of the workflow, so the number of clips to validate per site x species is a design decision. sheepdog offers two complementary views of it:

  • Stage 2, calibration_effort(). The cross-validated AUC of a calibration model as a function of the number of reviewed clips per site x species cell. It answers whether, pooled over all cells, more clips would still improve the calibration.
  • Stage 1, precision_by_bin() and suggest_thresholds(). Precision by confidence bin and the lowest threshold that reaches a target precision, for each site x species, with flags for bins and thresholds resting on few clips. They show which cells lack support.

This vignette runs both on the simulated example shipped with the package.

Example data

The example holds BirdNET predictions simulated for five frog species at four sites over six months (data-raw/make_example_data.R in the source repository). False-positive confidences overlap those of true detections, and false-positive rates differ among species and sites. The reviewed clips were drawn with the "top" design (the two highest confidences per site x species x night x hour, up to 80 clips per site x species) and their verdicts come from the simulated truth.

library(sheepdog)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

ex <- system.file("extdata", "example", package = "sheepdog")
val_files <- list.files(file.path(ex, "validation"), full.names = TRUE)
basename(val_files)
#> [1] "validation_by_clip_ARA.csv" "validation_by_clip_BAI.csv"
#> [3] "validation_by_clip_NHE.csv" "validation_by_clip_XAR.csv"

read_validations() stacks the tables and keeps the clips with a verdict and a confidence score, in the form used by the calibration models:

val <- read_validations(val_files)
#> 1600 reviewed clips (809 TP / 791 FP) of 5 species at 4 sites.
val |>
  summarise(precision = round(mean(tp), 2), .by = c(site, species)) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = species, values_from = precision)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   site  boa_ran den_nan lep_fus pse_pla sci_nas
#>   <fct>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 ARA      0.92    0.92    0.58    0.31    0.5 
#> 2 BAI      0.92    0.46    0.26    0.28    0.4 
#> 3 NHE      0.88    0.76    0       0.14    0.36
#> 4 XAR      0.78    0.68    0.38    0.28    0.31

The table gives the share of true positives among the reviewed clips of each cell (20 cells of 80 clips). It already shows that the same design yields very different precision across species and sites.

Stage 2: the effort curve

How the curve is built

For each training size n in n_train, calibration_effort() draws n clips from every site x species cell (keeping at least five per cell for testing), fits the model to the drawn clips and computes the AUC on all the remaining clips. This is repeated n_reps times per n; repetitions whose fit fails, or with fewer than 50 test clips, are dropped. The result gives, for each n, the mean and standard deviation of the AUC across repetitions.

The candidate formulas come from calibration_models(), and compare_calibration_models() ranks them by 5-fold cross-validation on all the clips (formulas with random effects need the ‘lme4’ package):

models <- calibration_models()
cv <- compare_calibration_models(val, models)
#> Cross-validation (5 folds) of 5 models...
select(cv, model, auc_mean, auc_sd)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   model                auc_mean auc_sd
#>   <chr>                   <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 m4_species_x_site       0.885 0.0181
#> 2 m3_plus_site            0.882 0.0194
#> 3 m2_species_slope        0.872 0.0183
#> 4 m1_species_intercept    0.865 0.0221
#> 5 m0_global               0.804 0.0256

The effort curve below is drawn for the global model (m0_global, a single logistic regression on the logit of the score) and for the hierarchical m4_species_x_site (random slopes by species and a site x species intercept), the structure used by FrogNet.

The vignette uses few repetitions so that it renders quickly. In real use keep the default of 50 repetitions (or more): the standard deviation is itself estimated from n_reps values and is unstable with few repetitions. Training sizes must stay below the size of the smallest cell minus five, since at most n - 5 clips of a cell are used for training whatever the value of n_train.

n_train <- c(5, 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 70)
n_reps  <- 15

The two curves 

eff_m0 <- calibration_effort(val, models$m0_global,
                             n_train = n_train, n_reps = n_reps)
#> Effort curve (15 repetitions per n)...
eff_m0
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   n_per_cell auc_mean  auc_sd
#>        <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1          5    0.803 0.00291
#> 2         10    0.803 0.00361
#> 3         20    0.803 0.00692
#> 4         30    0.802 0.00684
#> 5         45    0.808 0.0103 
#> 6         60    0.808 0.0148 
#> 7         70    0.795 0.0236
eff_m4 <- calibration_effort(val, models$m4_species_x_site,
                             n_train = n_train, n_reps = n_reps)
#> Effort curve (15 repetitions per n)...
eff_m4
#> # A tibble: 7 × 3
#>   n_per_cell auc_mean  auc_sd
#>        <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1          5    0.855 0.0104 
#> 2         10    0.870 0.00503
#> 3         20    0.875 0.00625
#> 4         30    0.881 0.00608
#> 5         45    0.887 0.00905
#> 6         60    0.883 0.0115 
#> 7         70    0.887 0.0153

The draws depend only on seed, n_train, n_reps and the data, not on the formula, so with the same arguments both curves are computed on the same training and test sets and can be compared repetition by repetition.

effort <- bind_rows(m0_global = eff_m0,
                    m4_species_x_site = if (has_lme4) eff_m4,
                    .id = "model")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(effort, aes(n_per_cell, auc_mean, colour = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = auc_mean - auc_sd, ymax = auc_mean + auc_sd),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Reviewed clips per site x species (training)",
       y = "Cross-validated AUC (mean ± sd)", colour = "Model") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Reading the curve

Which formula. The curve belongs to a model, not to the data. The mean AUC of the global model stays between 0.795 and 0.808 at every training size: it has only two parameters, which are estimated well from a few clips per cell, and more clips cannot correct its structural limitation, that one score-to-probability curve is shared by all species and sites. The hierarchical model starts higher (0.855 with 5 clips per cell) and keeps improving (0.875 with 20 and 0.887 with 70), because each additional clip also informs the species- and site-specific terms. The gap between the curves is the gain from modelling how species and sites differ; its size, not only the height of either curve, is what the choice of formula rests on. Draw the curve for the formula that compare_calibration_models() selects (or that calibrate() refits), with m0_global as a baseline.

Where it flattens. Beyond the training size at which the mean AUC stops increasing, extra clips in every cell add little discrimination. With a tolerance of 0.005 below the best mean AUC of each curve (an illustrative choice, not a rule of the package), the global model is flat from 10 clips per cell and the hierarchical model from 45. For the hierarchical model the gain per clip falls with effort: the first 5 extra clips per cell (from 5 to 10) add 0.015 to the mean AUC, and the next 35 (from 10 to 45) add 0.017 in total. The first clips of a cell fix its intercept and slope; the later ones only refine them. Small dips in the mean between neighbouring training sizes are within the spread of the repetitions and should not be read as losses.

The variability across repetitions. At small n the standard deviation measures how much the calibration depends on which clips were reviewed; a large spread means that a single validation round of that size may produce a poor model by chance. At large n the spread grows for a different reason: the test set is what is left of each cell, so it shrinks as n grows (with 70 training clips per cell, only 200 of the 1600 clips are left for testing). The right end of the curve is therefore estimated less precisely than its middle.

AUC measures discrimination (whether true detections score higher than false ones), not whether the calibrated probabilities are accurate. A curve that has flattened does not imply that the species- or site-specific curves of plot_calibration() are well estimated in every cell; that is what the per-cell view of stage 1 checks.

Stage 1: which cells lack support

The effort curve pools all cells. precision_by_bin() and suggest_thresholds() work cell by cell on the validation_by_clip.csv tables (the output of post_validation()), so they read the raw tables rather than the output of read_validations():

val_raw <- purrr::map(val_files, readr::read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()

prec <- precision_by_bin(val_raw, min_n = 15)
prec |>
  filter(site == "BAI", species_folder %in% c("lep_fus", "pse_pla")) |>
  mutate(precision = round(precision, 2)) |>
  select(species_folder, bin, n = n_reviewed, precision) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = species_folder,
                     values_from = c(n, precision))
#> # A tibble: 9 × 5
#>   bin       n_lep_fus n_pse_pla precision_lep_fus precision_pse_pla
#>   <fct>         <int>     <int>             <dbl>             <dbl>
#> 1 [0.1,0.2)        15         2              0                 0.5 
#> 2 [0.2,0.3)        15         7              0.2               0.43
#> 3 [0.3,0.4)        12         6              0.08              0.33
#> 4 [0.4,0.5)        11         8              0                 0.12
#> 5 [0.5,0.6)        10        15              0.4               0.07
#> 6 [0.6,0.7)        12        11              0.67              0.09
#> 7 [0.7,0.8)         3        14              1                 0.5 
#> 8 [0.8,0.9)         2        13              1                 0.15
#> 9 [0.9,1]          NA         4             NA                 1

A bin is flagged low_support when it holds fewer than min_n reviewed clips (here, bins with n below 15). The two cells shown fail in different ways. For lep_fus at BAI the few clips in the upper bins are all true positives, but those bins are flagged: the precision at high scores rests on a handful of clips. For pse_pla at BAI the upper bins hold more clips, and precision there is still low: the classifier confuses this species even at high scores.

suggest_thresholds() returns, for each cell, the lowest confidence at which precision reaches target_precision with at least min_n clips above it (NA when no cut does):

thr <- suggest_thresholds(val_raw, target_precision = 0.90, min_n = 15)
thr |>
  mutate(threshold = if_else(is.na(threshold), "-",
                             format(threshold, nsmall = 2))) |>
  select(site, species_folder, threshold) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = species_folder, values_from = threshold)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   site  boa_ran den_nan lep_fus pse_pla sci_nas
#>   <chr> <chr>   <chr>   <chr>   <chr>   <chr>  
#> 1 ARA   0.18    0.20    0.55    -       -      
#> 2 BAI   0.15    -       -       -       -      
#> 3 NHE   0.35    0.84    -       -       -      
#> 4 XAR   0.49    -       -       -       -

The target is reached in 7 of the 20 cells. A missing threshold has two possible causes, and they call for opposite decisions: too few reviewed clips at high scores (more review may help) or low precision even at high scores (more review will not). To tell them apart, count the high-score clips reviewed in each cell, their precision, and how many high-score detections in the complete selection tables were not reviewed:

conf_high <- 0.7   # example: what counts as a high score
min_n     <- 15

detections <- suppressMessages(
  read_selection_tables(file.path(ex, "birdnet"))) |>
  mutate(species = gsub("-", "_", sub("^.*_", "", species_code)))

support <- val |>
  mutate(across(c(site, species), as.character)) |>
  summarise(n_fp      = sum(tp == 0),
            n_high    = sum(confidence >= conf_high),
            prec_high = round(mean(tp[confidence >= conf_high]), 2),
            .by = c(site, species)) |>
  left_join(detections |>
              summarise(n_high_all = sum(confidence >= conf_high),
                        .by = c(site, species)),
            by = c("site", "species")) |>
  left_join(select(thr, site, species = species_folder, threshold),
            by = c("site", "species")) |>
  mutate(unreviewed_high = n_high_all - n_high,
         diagnosis = case_when(
           !is.na(threshold)        ~ "reached",
           unreviewed_high < min_n  ~ "exhausted",
           prec_high < 0.5          ~ "unreliable",
           .default = "review more"
         )) |>
  select(site, species, n_fp, n_high, prec_high, unreviewed_high,
         diagnosis) |>
  arrange(diagnosis, species, site)
print(support, n = Inf)
#> # A tibble: 20 × 7
#>    site  species  n_fp n_high prec_high unreviewed_high diagnosis  
#>    <chr> <chr>   <int>  <int>     <dbl>           <int> <chr>      
#>  1 BAI   lep_fus    59      5      1                  0 exhausted  
#>  2 NHE   lep_fus    80      3      0                  2 exhausted  
#>  3 XAR   lep_fus    50     10      1                  0 exhausted  
#>  4 ARA   boa_ran     6     62      0.97              87 reached    
#>  5 BAI   boa_ran     6     63      1                 97 reached    
#>  6 NHE   boa_ran    10     55      0.96             104 reached    
#>  7 XAR   boa_ran    18     50      0.96              84 reached    
#>  8 ARA   den_nan     6     48      0.98              65 reached    
#>  9 NHE   den_nan    19     54      0.85              85 reached    
#> 10 ARA   lep_fus    34     16      1                  1 reached    
#> 11 BAI   den_nan    43     27      0.81              28 review more
#> 12 XAR   den_nan    26     38      0.84              53 review more
#> 13 ARA   sci_nas    40     32      0.69              18 review more
#> 14 BAI   sci_nas    48     33      0.73              16 review more
#> 15 NHE   sci_nas    51     40      0.52              47 review more
#> 16 XAR   sci_nas    55     23      0.61              29 review more
#> 17 ARA   pse_pla    55     25      0.4               22 unreliable 
#> 18 BAI   pse_pla    58     31      0.42              20 unreliable 
#> 19 NHE   pse_pla    69     34      0.18              60 unreliable 
#> 20 XAR   pse_pla    58     36      0.33              36 unreliable

A cell is "reached" when suggest_thresholds() found a threshold. The other labels use illustrative cut-offs (conf_high, min_n and a precision of 0.5 at high scores); set them from the precision the study needs. In this example they separate three groups of cells that lack support:

  • "review more": den_nan at BAI, den_nan at XAR, sci_nas at ARA, sci_nas at BAI, sci_nas at NHE, sci_nas at XAR. Precision at high scores is intermediate and unreviewed high-score detections remain, so a further round of review restricted to high scores in these cells may reveal a cut that reaches the target.
  • "exhausted": lep_fus at BAI, lep_fus at NHE, lep_fus at XAR. The "top" design has already taken almost every high-score detection of these cells; more effort cannot add support. Treat the species at that site as poorly calibrated.
  • "unreliable": pse_pla at ARA, pse_pla at BAI, pse_pla at NHE, pse_pla at XAR. Most high-score detections are false positives; more review would only confirm it. These cells call for retraining the classifier (with the clips of retraining_clips()) rather than for more validation.

The column n_fp deserves a look of its own. The calibration slope is estimated from the contrast between true and false positives, so a cell with few false positives (here as few as 6) carries little information about the low end of its calibration curve, even with the same number of reviewed clips as the other cells. At the other extreme, a cell whose reviewed clips are all false positives (lep_fus at NHE) gives no information on true detections at all; it may be a site where the species is absent. These are interpretations of the model structure, not flags computed by the package.

The practical decision

Read the two views together:

  • If the effort curve of the chosen model is still rising at the current number of clips per cell, review more clips in every cell: the pooled calibration is limited by the overall effort.
  • If the curve has flattened but some cells lack support in stage 1, review more clips only in those cells, and target the confidence range where support is missing. Clips in cells that are already well supported add little.
  • If a cell is "exhausted" (no high-score detections left to review) or "unreliable" (low precision even at high scores), more validation cannot help. Treat the species at that site as poorly calibrated, as FrogNet did with the six species left out of the community matrices (see vignette("frognet-workflow")).

Two caveats apply. First, the curve depends on the formula: a hierarchical formula needs ‘lme4’, and its curve can differ markedly from that of the global model, so draw it for the model that will be used. Second, the curve depends on how the clips were chosen. The training and test clips of calibration_effort() are drawn from the same reviewed pool, so the AUC describes discrimination among clips selected by the same design. With the "top" design the pool over-represents high scores; the AUC is conditional on that design and is not an estimate of the false-positive rate of all detections. For that, use the "random_detections" design, which follows the observation-confirmation design of Chambert et al. (2015) (see vignette("crywolf-integration")).

The effort curve can also be drawn inside the whole calibration stage, with calibrate(..., effort_curve = TRUE); it is then computed for the best model of the cross-validation and written to effort_curve.csv. The arguments effort_n and effort_reps set the training sizes and the number of repetitions.

sites <- c("ARA", "BAI", "NHE", "XAR")
res <- calibrate(
  validation_files  = val_files,
  prediction_tables = setNames(
    file.path(ex, "birdnet", sites, "BirdNET_SelectionTable.txt"), sites),
  output_dir   = file.path(tempdir(), "calibration"),
  effort_curve = TRUE, effort_n = c(5, 10, 20, 30, 45, 60, 70),
  effort_reps  = 50
)
res$effort
